AWS added semantic config validation and per-hour throttling on host removal as remediations.

summary: Job Distribution Halted After DB Field Type Change
description: A deploy changed the type of a field in the PostgreSQL database used by the job-distribution service. Newly-written rows used the new type and old rows used the old type, so the distributor's strict schema validation failed on each scan and it stopped distributing work. Rolling back made the rows written between the two deploys unreadable, so distribution kept failing; recovery required hand-deploying a build that ignored the offending field, plus manual scaling.
symptoms: Job distribution service stopped assigning jobs
Schema validation errors logged by distributor
logs_signature: Job distribution service stopped assigning jobs, Schema validation errors logged by distributor, Builds remained queued without execution, Distributor scans failed repeatedly
root_cause: A deployment altered the type of a PostgreSQL field used by the job-distribution service, causing strict schema validation to fail on mixed-type rows.
resolution: A hand‑deployed build that ignored the offending field was released and manual scaling was applied to restore distribution.

But the GE system that was monitoring this had a bug which prevented the alarm from getting triggered, which eventually caused a cascading failure that eventually affected 55 million people.
logs_signature: missing alarms, cascading grid failure, 55 million people affected
root_cause: Transmission lines hit untrimmed foliage, and a bug in the GE monitoring system prevented the alarm from firing, so operators never redistributed power.

summary: Power disruption at GitHub primary datacenter
description: On January 28th, 2016 GitHub experienced a disruption in the power at their primary datacenter.
logs_signature: power disruption, site unavailable
root_cause: GitHub experienced a disruption in power at its primary datacenter.

summary: Lightning strikes cut power to GCE storage in europe-west1-b
description: Successive lightning strikes on their European datacenter (europe-west1-b) caused loss of power to Google Compute Engine storage systems within that region. I/O errors were observed on a subset of Standard Persistent Disks (HDDs) and permanent data loss was observed on a small fraction of those.
symptoms: permanent data loss on a small fraction
logs_signature: I/O errors on persistent disks, permanent data loss on a small fraction
root_cause: Successive lightning strikes caused loss of power to Compute Engine storage systems in the region.

summary: Redundant cooling failure in europe-west2-a data center
description: On Tuesday, 19 July 2022 at 06:33 US/Pacific, a simultaneous failure of multiple, redundant cooling systems in one of the data centers that hosts the zone europe-west2-a impacted multiple Google Cloud services. This resulted in some customers experiencing service unavailability for impacted products.
logs_signature: service unavailability, zone-wide impact
root_cause: Multiple redundant cooling systems failed simultaneously in a data center hosting the zone.

summary: Storage volume failure took down PythonAnywhere and hosted sites
description: A storage volume failure on one of storage servers caused a number of outages, starting with PythonAnywhere site and also with our users’ programs (including websites) that were dependent on that volume, and later spreading to other hosted sites.
logs_signature: site outage, user programs failing, outage spreading to other sites
root_cause: A storage volume failed on one of the storage servers, breaking everything that depended on it.

summary: Missing ECC in Sun servers caused corruption and crashes
description: Sun famously didn't include ECC in a couple generations of server parts. This resulted in data corruption and crashing. Following Sun's typical MO, they made customers that reported a bug sign an NDA before explaining the issue.
logs_signature: data corruption, server crashes
root_cause: Several generations of Sun server parts lacked ECC memory, leading to data corruption and crashes.

summary: DNS Enactor race left DynamoDB us-east-1 endpoint empty
description: A latent race condition in DynamoDB's DNS management left the regional endpoint `dynamodb.us-east-1.amazonaws.com` with an empty record. Two redundant "DNS Enactor" processes raced when one was unusually delayed; a second Enactor applied a newer plan and ran cleanup while the first overwrote the regional endpoint with a stale older plan, which the cleanup process then deleted. The DynamoDB outage cascaded into EC2 (DWFM "congestive collapse"), Network Load Balancer health-check flapping, and Lambda for ~15 hours.
symptoms: cascading EC2, NLB and Lambda failures for ~15 hours
logs_signature: DynamoDB endpoint unresolvable, cascading EC2, NLB and Lambda failures for ~15 hours
root_cause: Two DNS Enactor processes raced; a delayed one overwrote the regional endpoint with a stale plan, which cleanup then deleted, leaving an empty DNS record.

summary: Installer typo and name conflict deleted boot.ini
description: A typo and a name conflict caused the installer to sometimes delete the *boot.ini* file on installation of an expansion for *EVE Online* - with consequences.
logs_signature: user machines failing to boot
root_cause: A typo and a name conflict caused the EVE Online expansion installer to sometimes delete the boot.ini file.

summary: Switch upgrade froze network, fileserver pairs fenced each other
description: During an aggregation-switch ISSU upgrade, terminating an agent on one switch left the link up just long enough for the peer's MLAG failover to use the disruptive (rather than stateful) path, freezing the network for ~90 seconds. That spike caused fileserver Pacemaker/Heartbeat/DRBD pairs in different racks to exceed their heartbeats and STONITH each other, leaving many active/passive pairs with both nodes powered off; recovery required identifying the previously-active node from logs for each pair and took >5 hours.
logs_signature: network frozen ~90 seconds, fileserver pairs powered off
root_cause: During a switch ISSU upgrade the peer took the disruptive MLAG failover path; the network freeze made Pacemaker/DRBD pairs miss heartbeats and STONITH each other.
resolution: Recovery required identifying the previously-active node of each pair from logs and took over 5 hours.

summary: 43-second partition triggered MySQL failover with lost writes
description: A 43 second network partition during maintenance caused MySQL master failover, but the new master didn't have several seconds of writes propogated to it because of cross-continent latency.  24+ hours of restoration work to maintain data integrity.
logs_signature: MySQL master failover, inconsistent data
root_cause: A network partition during maintenance caused a MySQL master failover to a cross-continent replica that had not received several seconds of writes.
resolution: Over 24 hours of restoration work to preserve data integrity.

summary: Duplicate ZooKeeper leaders split Kafka into conflicting clusters
description: During routine ZooKeeper reprovisioning, replacement hosts were added too quickly and elected a second leader, creating two distinct ZooKeeper clusters. A Kafka broker for the background-job system connected to the new cluster and elected itself controller, so two Kafka clusters served conflicting state to clients; ~10% of background-job writes failed over 2h32m.
logs_signature: ~10% of background-job writes failed, conflicting cluster state
root_cause: Replacement ZooKeeper hosts were added too quickly and elected a second leader; a Kafka broker joined the new cluster and became controller, so two Kafka clusters served conflicting state.

summary: Fast migration plus long read query locked critical Postgres table
description: All queries on a critical PostgreSQL table were blocked by the combination of an extremely fast database migration and a long-running read query, causing 15 seconds of downtime.
logs_signature: all queries on table blocked, 15 seconds of downtime
root_cause: An extremely fast database migration combined with a long-running read query blocked all queries on a critical PostgreSQL table.

summary: Slow code path for load balancer changes froze public addressing
description: Many changes to a rarely modified load balancer were applied through a very slow code path. This froze all public addressing changes for ~2 hours.
logs_signature: public addressing changes frozen ~2 hours
root_cause: Many changes to a rarely modified load balancer were applied through a very slow code path, blocking other addressing changes.

summary: Fiber path component failure cut backbone bandwidth
description: A failure of a component on a fiber path from one of the central US gateway campuses in Google’s production backbone led to a decrease in available network bandwidth between the gateway and multiple edge locations, causing packet loss while the backbone automatically moved traffic onto remaining paths.
logs_signature: packet loss, reduced bandwidth to edge locations
root_cause: A component on a fiber path from a central US gateway campus failed, reducing bandwidth between the gateway and multiple edge locations.
resolution: The backbone automatically moved traffic onto the remaining paths.

summary: Postgres failover made incident IDs jump by 32
description: Customers noticed their per-organization `INC-N` IDs jumping by exactly 32 (e.g. `#INC-7` directly to `#INC-39`) after a Postgres HA upgrade that promoted a follower to primary. Postgres's `nextval` pre-allocates `SEQ_LOG_VALS = 32` sequence values on the WAL to avoid logging every `nextval`; a follower sees the post-crash state, so when promoted the sequence jumps forward by up to 32. Fix was to replace `nextval` with a `SELECT MAX(external_id)+1` trigger.
logs_signature: incident IDs skipping by 32
root_cause: Postgres pre-allocates 32 sequence values in the WAL; when a follower was promoted to primary during an HA upgrade, the sequence jumped forward.
resolution: Replaced nextval with a trigger computing MAX(external_id)+1.

summary: Conflicting deployed versions and reused flag caused $460M loss
description: A combination of conflicting deployed versions and re-using a previously used bit caused a $460M loss. See also a longer write-up.
logs_signature: unintended trading orders, massive financial loss
root_cause: Servers ran conflicting deployed versions and a previously used flag bit was re-used, activating old code.

summary: SHA-1 colliding test files broke deduplicated SVN repository
description: The WebKit repository, a Subversion repository configured to use deduplication, became unavailable after two files with the same SHA-1 hash were checked in as test data, with the intention of implementing a safety check for collisions. The two files had different md5 sums and so a checkout would fail a consistency check. For context, the first public SHA-1 hash collision had very recently been announced, with an example of two colliding files.
logs_signature: repository unavailable, checkouts failing consistency checks
root_cause: Two files with the same SHA-1 but different MD5 were committed as test data to a Subversion repository configured for deduplication.

summary: Leap-day date math created invalid certificates, global Azure outage
description: Certificates that were valid for one year were created. Instead of using an appropriate library, someone wrote code that computed one year to be the current date plus one year. On February 29th 2012, this resulted in the creation of certificates with an expiration date of February 29th 2013, which were rejected because of the invalid date. This caused an Azure global outage that lasted for most of a day.
symptoms: global outage for most of a day
logs_signature: certificates rejected, global outage for most of a day
root_cause: Code computed one-year certificate expiry as current date plus one year, so on Feb 29 2012 it created certificates expiring on the invalid date Feb 29 2013.

summary: Leap second made Go time go backwards and crash DNS resolver
description: Backwards time flow from tracking the 27th leap second on 2016-12-31T23:59:60Z caused the weighted round-robin selection of DNS resolvers (RRDNS) to panic and fail on some CNAME lookups.  Go's `time.Now()` was incorrectly assumed to be monotonic; this injected negative values into calls to `rand.Int63n()`, which panics in that case.
logs_signature: RRDNS panics, failed CNAME lookups
root_cause: Go's time.Now() was assumed monotonic; the leap second produced negative durations passed to rand.Int63n(), which panics.

summary: Leap second printk deadlocked Linux kernel on xtime_lock
description: Leap second code was called from the timer interrupt handler, which held `xtime_lock`. That code did a `printk` to log the leap second. `printk` wakes up `klogd`, which can sometimes try to get the time, which waits on `xtime_lock`, causing a deadlock.
logs_signature: kernel deadlock, system hang
root_cause: Leap second code ran in the timer interrupt holding xtime_lock and called printk, which woke klogd, which waited on xtime_lock.

summary: Leap second rewind made timers fire early, causing CPU spin
description: When a leap second occurred, `CLOCK_REALTIME` was rewound by one second. This was not done via a mechanism that would update `hrtimer base.offset`. This meant that when a timer interrupt happened, TIMER_ABSTIME CLOCK_REALTIME timers got expired one second early, including timers set for less than one second. This caused applications that used sleep for less than one second in a loop to spinwait without sleeping, causing high load on many systems. This caused a large number of web services to go down in 2012.
logs_signature: high CPU load, applications spin-waiting, many web services down
root_cause: CLOCK_REALTIME was rewound without updating hrtimer base.offset, so absolute timers expired a second early and short sleep loops spun without sleeping.

summary: Expired intermediate certificate disabled all Firefox add-ons
description: Most Firefox add-ons stopped working around May 4th 2019 when a certificate expired. Firefox requires a valid certificate chain to prevent malware. About nine hours later, Mozilla pushed a privileged add-on that injected a valid certificate into Firefox's certificate store, creating a valid chain and unblocking add-ons. This disabled effectively all add-ons, about 15,000, and the resolution took approximately 15-21 hours for most users. Some user data was lost. Previously Mozilla posted about the technical details.
logs_signature: ~15,000 add-ons disabled, certificate chain invalid, some user data lost
root_cause: A certificate in the add-on signing chain expired, and Firefox requires a valid chain for add-ons.
resolution: About nine hours later Mozilla pushed a privileged add-on that injected a valid certificate, restoring the chain; full resolution took 15-21 hours for most users.

summary: Primary database overloaded by queued operations at peak
description: At peak Wednesday-afternoon load, the primary database backed up with queued operations to the point that it stopped catching up; rolling back recent changes had no isolated effect because the queue depth had already saturated the system, and a primary failover to kill queued ops only bought temporary headroom. After the runnable-queue was drained, builds were stuck in the prior queue stage; manually promoting them flooded the next queue, and the build-scheduler's failure-mode throttles fired on what were actually normal conditions and backed off precisely when more throughput was needed. CircleCI rebuilt tooling on the fly to clear a 17-hour backlog.
logs_signature: database queue saturated, builds stuck, 17-hour backlog
root_cause: At peak load the primary database backed up with queued operations and could not catch up; throttles then fired on normal conditions and reduced throughput.
resolution: A failover gave temporary headroom and the team rebuilt tooling on the fly to clear the backlog.

summary: Stale planner statistics after DB upgrade forced full disk scans
description: A blue/green upgrade of the workflows database succeeded mechanically, but the post-cutover database was running every query against disk because its statistics tables had not been updated. The team ran `ANALYZE` early in the upgrade procedure, but a second major-version upgrade in the same deployment then made those statistics stale, leaving the planner without usable indexes after the cutover. Workflows latency spiked, jobs were dropped after exhausting their 10-minute retry, and the team eventually re-promoted the old (blue) database to recover.
logs_signature: workflow latency spike, jobs dropped after retries
root_cause: A second major-version upgrade made earlier ANALYZE statistics stale, so after cutover the planner ran every query against disk without usable indexes.
resolution: The team re-promoted the old (blue) database to recover.

summary: Migration load and Pacemaker segfault caused split-brain MySQL
description: A schema migration produced enough load that Percona Replication Manager failed the MySQL master over to a node with a cold InnoDB buffer pool, which then failed back. Disabling Pacemaker `maintenance-mode` the next day triggered a Pacemaker segfault that produced a partition; two simultaneous master elections occurred and the elected primary was the stale node, allowing 7 minutes of data drift in which 16 private repositories were briefly routed to the wrong owners.
symptoms: private repos routed to wrong owners
logs_signature: unexpected master failovers, data drift, private repos routed to wrong owners
root_cause: Migration load triggered failover to a cold node; next day a Pacemaker segfault caused a partition and two elections chose a stale primary.

summary: systemd capped file descriptors, causing ProxySQL meltdowns
description: The `mysql1` cluster experienced four ProxySQL meltdowns over nine days: an analytics query hitting the master instead of replicas, a planned promotion that recreated the failure, and then two load-driven incidents revealing that systemd had silently capped `LimitNOFILE` from 1,073,741,824 to 65,536 because of a kernel-level limit of 1,048,576. Total impact was 8h14m across the four incidents.
logs_signature: repeated ProxySQL failures, 8h14m total impact
root_cause: An analytics query hit the master, and systemd silently capped LimitNOFILE to 65,536 because of a kernel limit, so ProxySQL ran out of descriptors under load.

summary: Foreign key hit INT32 max, breaking Actions and Pages
description: A foreign key on the scoped-tokens table hit max INT32, causing high failure rates for Actions and Pages and breaking scoped-token Git operations for 9h48m. Mitigation required a long-running schema migration to INT64. Linting that would have caught the column predated the column itself; one Action briefly received unauthorized access grants that were then revoked.
symptoms: high Actions and Pages failure rates
logs_signature: high Actions and Pages failure rates, scoped-token Git operations failing
root_cause: A foreign key on the scoped-tokens table reached the maximum INT32 value.
resolution: Mitigated with a long-running schema migration to INT64.

summary: Peak load exhausted ProxySQL connections on mysql1
description: Peak-hour load on the shared `mysql1` cluster repeatedly exhausted ProxySQL connections over a week, requiring four primary failovers plus an emergency index and proactive throttling of webhooks and Actions. Memory profiling turned on to debug performance later triggered another connection failure, requiring yet another failover.
logs_signature: connection exhaustion, repeated primary failovers
root_cause: Peak-hour load on the shared mysql1 cluster repeatedly exhausted ProxySQL connections; later memory profiling triggered another failure.
resolution: Four primary failovers, an emergency index and proactive throttling of webhooks and Actions.

summary: Three database incidents in three days degraded GitHub
description: May 9: a connection-saturation config rollout to the Git database triggered a failover; the rollback then failed due to an internal infrastructure error, causing >10h of degraded pull-request/push consistency. May 10: an inefficient GitHub App permissions API endpoint with a retry-on-timeout caller produced a 7× write-latency spike on the auth-token cluster, peaking at 76% token-issuance failure. May 11: a Git database crash auto-failed-over but the read replicas weren't reattached, leaving the primary unable to serve full read load.
logs_signature: degraded push and PR consistency, write-latency spike, 76% token-issuance failures
root_cause: A connection-saturation config rollout triggered a failover with failed rollback, an inefficient retrying API endpoint spiked write latency, and a crash failover left read replicas detached.

summary: Shorter cache TTL plus rising reads overwhelmed auth database
description: Two popular client apps had been quietly increasing read traffic 10×, then a Saturday change shortened a user-settings cache TTL from 12h to 2h. On Monday's peak, the combined write amplification from cache rewrites plus read load overwhelmed the core auth/user-management database cluster, cascading through every service that depends on it (github.com, API, Actions, Git over HTTPS, Copilot, etc.).
symptoms: site, API, Actions and Git failures
logs_signature: auth database overloaded, site, API, Actions and Git failures
root_cause: Client read traffic had grown 10x and a change shortened a user-settings cache TTL from 12h to 2h; combined write amplification and reads overwhelmed the auth database cluster.

summary: Table rename in schema migration deadlocked MySQL read replicas
description: The GitHub platform encountered a novel failure mode when processing a schema migration on a large MySQL table. Schema migrations are a common task at GitHub and often take weeks to complete. The final step in a migration is to perform a rename to move the updated table into the correct place. During the final step of this migration a significant portion of our MySQL read replicas entered a semaphore deadlock. Our MySQL clusters consist of a primary node for write traffic, multiple read replicas for production traffic, and several replicas that serve internal read traffic for backup and analytics purposes. The read replicas that hit the deadlock entered a crash-recovery state causing an increased load on healthy read replicas. Due to the cascading nature of this scenario, there were not enough active read replicas to handle production requests which impacted the availability of core GitHub services.
logs_signature: read replicas in crash recovery, core services unavailable
root_cause: During the final rename step of a schema migration many MySQL read replicas hit a semaphore deadlock, overloading the remaining healthy replicas.

summary: Foreign key type smaller than primary key overflowed, Heroku API down
description: At 15:05 UTC on June 8, 2023, a database error occurred where a foreign key used a smaller data type than the primary key that it referenced. This error caused an overflow when the primary key exceeded the allowable value, resulting in an inability to create new authorizations within Heroku. This error also prevented customers from creating new deployments. The oncall operations then triggered the Heroku API full outage.
logs_signature: new authorizations failing, deployments blocked, full API outage
root_cause: A foreign key used a smaller data type than the primary key it referenced and overflowed when the key exceeded its limit.

summary: Unneeded transactions exhausted Go database connection pool
description: Two weeks of intermittent app timeouts, with traces showing requests waiting up to 20s for a connection from Go's `database/sql` pool, but contention spread across many endpoints rather than a single slow query. After 24 deploys' worth of fixes (materialized views, indexes, lock timeouts, async Slack-webhook handling, and a custom `ngrok/sqlmw` middleware to attribute connection-pool hold time per operation), the root cause turned out to be an unnecessary transaction wrapping every Slack modal submission — many small fast transactions were in aggregate exhausting the pool.
logs_signature: intermittent app timeouts, 20s waits for DB connections
root_cause: An unnecessary transaction wrapped every Slack modal submission; many small transactions together exhausted the connection pool.
resolution: Found after adding per-operation pool-hold-time instrumentation and removed the unnecessary transaction.

summary: PGAudit hung holding locks during routine migration
description: After a Postgres 17 upgrade the weekend before, PGAudit was re-enabled based on staging testing. A routine migration to create an empty table and add an index triggered a pathological interaction with PGAudit: the extension hung while holding critical locks, ignored timeout signals, and blocked other DB operations across the dashboard, mobile app, Slack app, and API. The primary was restarted to break the deadlock (~2 minutes hard outage), then PGAudit was removed entirely.
logs_signature: database operations blocked, dashboard, app and API down
root_cause: After a Postgres 17 upgrade, PGAudit hung while holding critical locks during an index creation and ignored timeout signals.
resolution: The primary was restarted to break the deadlock and PGAudit was removed.

summary: Async task processing subsystem failure broke cart and bulk edits
description: The Allegro platform suffered a failure of a subsystem responsible for asynchronous distributed task processing. The problem affected many areas, e.g. features such as purchasing numerous offers via cart and bulk offer editing (including price list editing) did not work at all. Moreover, it partially failed to send daily newsletter with new offers. Also some parts of internal administration panel were affected.
logs_signature: cart purchases failing, bulk edits not working, newsletter partially failed
root_cause: The subsystem responsible for asynchronous distributed task processing failed.

summary: Typo in S3 debugging command removed critical servers
description: Human error. On February 28th 2017 9:37AM PST, the Amazon S3 team was debugging a minor issue. Despite using an established playbook, one of the commands intending to remove a small number of servers was issued with a typo, inadvertently causing a larger set of servers to be removed. These servers supported critical S3 systems. As a result, dependent systems required a full restart to correctly operate, and the system underwent widespread outages for US-EAST-1 (Northern Virginia) until final resolution at 1:54PM PST. Since Amazon's own services such as EC2 and EBS rely on S3 as well, it caused a vast cascading failure which affected hundreds of companies.
symptoms: cascading failures across AWS and customers
logs_signature: S3 outage in US-EAST-1, cascading failures across AWS and customers
root_cause: A command meant to remove a few servers was issued with a typo and removed a larger set supporting critical S3 systems.
resolution: Dependent systems needed a full restart; the issue was resolved at 1:54 PM PST.

summary: Message corruption overwhelmed S3 request processing fleet
description: Message corruption caused the distributed server state function to overwhelm resources on the S3 request processing fleet.
logs_signature: S3 request processing overloaded
root_cause: Message corruption caused the distributed server state function to overwhelm resources on the S3 request processing fleet.

summary: Networking upgrade error caused resource crunch in US East
description: Human error during a routine networking upgrade led to a resource crunch, exacerbated by software bugs, that ultimately resulted in an outage across all US East Availability Zones as well as a loss of 0.07% of volumes.
logs_signature: outage across US East AZs, 0.07% of volumes lost
root_cause: Human error during a routine networking upgrade caused a resource crunch, made worse by software bugs.

summary: Latent memory leak in EBS reporting agent exhausted memory
description: Inability to contact a data collection server triggered a latent memory leak bug in the reporting agent on the storage servers. And there is no graceful degradation handling, thus the reporting agent continuously contacted the collection server in a way that slowly consumed system memory. Also the monitoring system failed to alarm this EBS server's memory leak, also EBS servers generally make very dynamic use of all memory. By Monday morning, the rate of memory loss became quite high and confused enough memory on the affected storage servers which cannot keep with the request handling process. This error got further severed by the inability to do the failover, which resulted in the outage.
logs_signature: storage servers out of memory, requests not handled, EBS outage
root_cause: Failing to contact a data collection server triggered a memory leak in the reporting agent, which kept retrying and slowly consumed memory; monitoring did not alarm and failover failed.

summary: Maintenance process accidentally run against production ELB state
description: Elastic Load Balancer ran into problems when "a maintenance process that was inadvertently run against the production ELB state data".
logs_signature: load balancer failures
root_cause: A maintenance process was inadvertently run against the production Elastic Load Balancer state data.

summary: Network disruption overloaded metadata service, nodes retried forever
description: A "network disruption" caused metadata services to experience load that caused response times to exceed timeout values, causing storage nodes to take themselves down. Nodes that took themselves down continued to retry, ensuring that load on metadata services couldn't decrease.
logs_signature: metadata service timeouts, storage nodes taking themselves down
root_cause: A network disruption overloaded metadata services; storage nodes that timed out took themselves down and kept retrying, so load never decreased.

summary: Scaling Kinesis cache fleet exceeded OS thread limit
description: Scaling the front-end cache fleet for Kinesis caused all of the servers in the fleet to exceed the maximum number of threads allowed by an operating system configuration. Multiple critical downstream services affected, from Cognito to Lambda to CloudWatch.
logs_signature: Kinesis front-end failures, Cognito, Lambda and CloudWatch impacted
root_cause: Adding capacity to the front-end cache fleet made every server exceed the maximum number of threads allowed by an OS configuration.

summary: Automated scaling triggered connection surge congesting AWS network
description: At 7:30 AM PST, an automated activity to scale capacity of one of the AWS services hosted in the main AWS network triggered an unexpected behavior from a large number of clients inside the internal network. This resulted in a large surge of connection activity that overwhelmed the networking devices between the internal network and the main AWS network, resulting in delays for communication between these networks. These delays increased latency and errors for services communicating between these networks, resulting in even more connection attempts and retries. This led to persistent congestion and performance issues on the devices connecting the two networks.
symptoms: errors between internal and main networks
logs_signature: increased latency, errors between internal and main networks, retry storms
root_cause: An automated capacity-scaling activity triggered a surge of client connections that overwhelmed the networking devices between the internal and main AWS networks.

summary: Power loss on storage nodes cascaded via aggressive handshake timeouts
description: Multiple SimpleDB storage nodes lost power simultaneously in one US-East data center. The lock service de-registered them rapidly, which spiked load and pushed handshake latencies above SimpleDB's too-aggressive handshake timeout. Healthy storage and metadata nodes failed their handshakes, removed themselves from the cluster, and couldn't rejoin because the metadata nodes that would authorize them had also taken themselves out. Recovery required manually raising the handshake timeout and restarting metadata nodes.
logs_signature: SimpleDB unavailable, nodes removed from cluster
root_cause: Simultaneous power loss on storage nodes spiked load so handshake latency exceeded an aggressive timeout; healthy nodes then removed themselves and could not rejoin.
resolution: Recovered by manually raising the handshake timeout and restarting metadata nodes.

summary: Packet signature triggered latent bug in Direct Connect devices
description: A new failover-optimization protocol had been enabled in network device OS for 8 months without issue. A customer traffic pattern produced packets matching a very specific signature that triggered a latent defect in the OS, causing devices in one Direct Connect network layer to fail. Failed devices weren't automatically removed from service, so engineers manually drained them, only for additional devices to fail with the same bug. Disabling the new protocol restored Direct Connect to Tokyo after ~6 hours.
logs_signature: Direct Connect devices failing, Tokyo connectivity lost ~6 hours
root_cause: A specific customer packet signature triggered a latent defect in a new failover-optimization protocol in the network device OS.
resolution: Engineers drained failed devices and finally disabled the new protocol, restoring service.

summary: Lambda cell crossed new capacity threshold, triggering latent bug
description: As the Lambda Frontend fleet scaled in response to normal daily traffic growth, it crossed a capacity threshold within a single cell that had never been reached before, triggering a latent software defect that caused Execution Environments to be successfully allocated but never fully utilized. Lambda invocations failed in the affected cell, cascading into STS, EKS, EventBridge, Connect, and the AWS Management Console for several hours.
symptoms: STS, EKS, EventBridge and Console degraded
logs_signature: Lambda invocations failing, STS, EKS, EventBridge and Console degraded
root_cause: As the Lambda Frontend fleet scaled, one cell crossed a never-reached capacity threshold that triggered a defect leaving execution environments allocated but unused.

summary: Uneven shard distribution caused Kinesis redistribution storm
description: A Kinesis cell newly migrated to a new architecture had an unusually high number of very low-throughput shards. The cell management system distributed the shards unevenly, so a few hosts ended up handling huge numbers of shards and produced abnormally large status messages. The system misinterpreted slow status messages as host failures, kicked off a redistribution storm, and overloaded the secure-connection provisioning subsystem. CloudWatch Logs, S3 event notifications, Firehose, ECS, Lambda, Redshift, MWAA, and Glue all degraded for ~7 hours.
symptoms: CloudWatch Logs, Lambda and others impacted
logs_signature: Kinesis degraded ~7 hours, CloudWatch Logs, Lambda and others impacted
root_cause: Shards were distributed unevenly, producing huge status messages that were misread as host failures, triggering a redistribution storm that overloaded connection provisioning.

summary: Double free triggered by database update crashed all servers
description: A double free revealed by a database update caused all "impression bus" servers to crash simultaneously. This wasn't caught in staging and made it into production because a time delay is required to trigger the bug, and the staging period didn't have a built-in delay.
symptoms: all impression bus servers crashed simultaneously
logs_signature: all impression bus servers crashed simultaneously
root_cause: A database update revealed a double free bug; it needed a time delay to trigger, so staging did not catch it.

summary: Race in switch code caused cascading phone network reboots
description: A bad line of C code introduced a race hazard which in due course collapsed the phone network. After a planned outage, the quickfire resumption messages triggered the race,  causing more reboots which retriggered the problem. "The problem repeated iteratively throughout the 114 switches in the network, blocking over 50 million calls in the nine hours it took to stabilize the system." From 1990.
symptoms: 50 million calls blocked over nine hours
logs_signature: switches repeatedly rebooting, 50 million calls blocked over nine hours
root_cause: A bad line of C code introduced a race that was triggered by rapid resumption messages, causing reboots that retriggered the problem across 114 switches.

summary: 775 Atlassian customers lost access for up to 14 days
description: On Tuesday, April 5th, 2022, starting at 7:38 UTC, 775 Atlassian customers lost access to their Atlassian products. The outage spanned up to 14 days for a subset of these customers, with the first set of customers being restored on April 8th and all customer sites progressively restored by April 18th.
logs_signature: customer sites inaccessible, multi-day outage
root_cause: 775 customers lost access to their Atlassian products; the summary does not state the cause.
resolution: Customer sites were progressively restored between April 8th and April 18th.

summary: Database hit integer limit, Basecamp went read-only
description: In November 2018 a database hit the integer limit, leaving the service in read-only mode. Same-day status update during the incident: signalvnoise.com.
logs_signature: service in read-only mode, writes failing
root_cause: A database column hit its integer limit.

summary: Overloaded database throttled requests, uncached BBC services failed
